speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR OPENING OF TOURIST OFFICE IN SAN FRANCISCO, CAL.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. This question I raise is important to the tourist council of British Columbia, chambers of commerce and others because of the nearness of summer.
In view of the need for the widest possible dissemination of information in the United States with respect to the recreational opportunities provided in Canada for tourists, and in view of the representations made to the minister by the British Columbia tourist council urging the establishment of a Canadian government tourist office in San Francisco, would the minister inform the house whether it is the government's intention to establish a Canadian government tourist office in San Francisco?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister of Northern Affairs and Natural Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: REQUEST FOR OPENING OF TOURIST OFFICE IN SAN FRANCISCO, CAL.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the	hon.
member for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question. At the present time there are government tourist offices in the cities of Chicago and New York. The proposal to set up an office in San Francisco was made in the standing committee on mines, forests and waters of last year, along with recommendations for facilities in three other cities. The government looked at all these recommendations and did accept the proposition that increased efforts had to be made to attract tourists from the United States into Canada, and therefore increased the amount of money available to this branch of the department.

But in the priorities we had to work out, the best method of getting more for our money was the test. We decided it should be through direct advertising so as to have an impact effect on the United States markets. In the efforts to get at certain other sections of the market we had to decide that San Francisco could not be provided with an office at this time. Therefore there will not be any office opened this year in San Francisco.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR OPENING OF TOURIST OFFICE IN SAN FRANCISCO, CAL.
speechtext: As a supplementary question, can I ask the minister whether it is not a fact that treasury board rejected this proposal?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: REQUEST FOR OPENING OF TOURIST OFFICE IN SAN FRANCISCO, CAL.
speechtext: The government had this matter under consideration, and treasury board is still part of the government.

speechtext:
I should like to ask the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs-and may I express the pleasure of all the people of British

Inquiries of the Ministry Columbia that at long last the hon. gentleman's abilities have been recognized-the following question. In view of an article appearing in the magazine Modern Car Engineering and an article in the Ottawa Citizen of April 23 written by Mr. Lynch, would the minister inform the house whether it is a fact that we are two years behind in the construction of the atomic research reactor being provided to India under the Colombo plan because of the so-called bungling of Canadians? If so, can the minister explain the reason for being so far behind schedule?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: REPORTED DELAY IN CONSTRUC- TION OF INDIAN REACTOR
speechtext:
I thank the hon. gentleman for having given me notice of this question about alleged delays in the construction of the atomic research reactor being provided to India by Canada under the Colombo plan.
In view of recent reports in the daily press and elsewhere about this reactor, I wish to take this opportunity to assure the house that in so far as there have been any delays in relation to the original target date, which in the very nature of things could be no more than an estimate, these are in no way attributable to any bungling by either Canadian or Indian participants in this worth-while project. Any delays that were experienced- and these have long since been completely overcome-were due to the complex nature of the project and the unusual type of structure involved.
I might mention also that this project is now very close to completion and, in fact, the plant is expected to be activated within a matter of weeks. We have been assured by the Indian authorities that they are in all respects fully and completely satisfied with the co-operation they have received from Canada in connection with this project.

Today, I should like to add a few remarks to express the satisfaction felt by the people of Sherbrooke over that new method of financing Canadian universities, and to say a word too about the contradictory and opportunist attitude of the Liberals with regard to this matter. Finally, I will admit that Bill C-56 constitutes an important step towards the gradual return to the provinces of their taxation powers, which will allow them, after having been placed under an economic trusteeship under the Liberal regime, to gradually recover, under the Conservative administration, their constitutional majority and responsibility.
Mr. Speaker, the people of Sherbrooke,, the electors, both men and women, whom I represent, the population of the eastern townships or Estrie, are particularly interested in that part of the project which regards the financing of universities.

In order to spend the amounts of money which they had secured, and with which they did not want to part, the Liberals interfered in provincial fields such as education which, under section 93 of the Canadian constitution, belongs exclusively to the provinces.

By short changing the provinces, the Liberal party had also short changed the universities. All they could do was either accept grants from Ottawa or else go bankrupt. In 1951 all Canadian universities fell for it and were financially compelled to accept Liberal grants. But from 1952 on, Quebec universities became wise to the fact that the Liberals were out to sacrifice the higher principle of exclusive provincial jurisdiction in the field of education and turned down those grants.
That is how the Liberal party, while preaching national unity, introduced legislation aimed at short changing the provinces, at creating differences among them and at confusing Canadian opinion on many issues.
And the same Liberal supporters, now very few in Ottawa and fighting a losing battle in Quebec with Mr. Jean Lesage, would have the present Conservative government solve, within a few short years, the complicated problems created by their own party.

I shall not say what I have in mind. During the debate on this legislation, we heard, among others, a speech by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion).
Before saying what I think of his remarks, may I say that I have great regard and admiration for the hon. member for Bellechasse. I admire him very much and I think that what has been written about him in a certain Montreal weekly is downright disgusting.
If there is a Conservative member from Quebec who would deserve to be a cabinet
Dominion-Provincial Relations member, it is the hon. member for Bellechasse, and I say this even though I do not share his political views.
At the outset of his speech on this legislation, the hon. member said-and, for the information of the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville, this quotation may be found on page 14 of the appendix to Hansard of April 26, 1960:
In consequence-though it may displease those who do not share my opinion, and with all due respect for the views of others-I want to confirm once more, at the very beginning of my remarks, that federal grants to our institutions of higher learning in this country are obviously inconsistent with the imperative principles of our constitution and contrary to the rights, powers and obligations which are an exclusively provincial field.
In short, the hon. member for Bellechasse told us, in a somewhat mitigated form, that federal grants to universities are unconstitutional.
This bill contains Mr. St. Laurent's formula, a formula, as you well know, Mr. Speaker, that did not impose any condition on the provinces nor on the universities. On the other hand, the present legislation, in addition to the St. Laurent formula, contains certain conditions.
In the first place, it is the federal government that is telling the Quebec and other provincial governments who want to take advantage of that legislation how a tax can be levied by a province for a provincial purpose.
In the second place, the federal government itself decides how part of the tax will be used to meet that provincial purpose.
Third, as the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) pointed out a few moments ago, the Minister of Finance of the federal government is to be the ultimate judge with regard to the distribution and use of that provincial tax, levied within the limits of the jurisdiction of Quebec and other provinces wishing to avail themselves of the act.
The hon. member for Bellechasse also mentioned on several occasions in this house that he had much apprehension with regard to precedent in British law.
Now, in spite of this fear and apprehension, he is still urging his Conservative colleagues from the province of Quebec to support this bill, and for two reasons.
We have inherited a situation created by the former administration, says he-and I

Dominion-Provincial Relations repeat, the former administration-and the legislation we are about to accept as a solution, at this time, will only be temporary.
I would have liked to repeat here, Mr. Speaker, the remark made to me by someone who has never had university training, and who was talking to me about the attitude of the hon. member for Bellechasse, but I will tell him about it privately.
The fact remains that the attitude of the Conservative members from the province of Quebec-

speechtext:
I am amazed, not to say flabbergasted, at the present attitude of the Conservatives from Quebec and of the representatives of the Quebec government.
For years, they made provincial autonomy their battle cry, for obvious political purposes.
It was a mock autonomy, an inactive but convenient autonomy which helped them beg for votes.
The Conservatives from Quebec, at a conference a few months ago, asked, urged, the government to find a formula. Why were they urging the government to find a formula? This is due to the fact that they were feeling out public opinion in our province and discovering that the population had enough of seeing them play politics with a principle such as that of autonomy.
The Conservative government in Ottawa has always proclaimed its respect for our constitution. It developed a formula or rather, according to the press, the former premier of Quebec, Mr. Sauve, for whom I had the greatest respect, submitted a formula verbally -and one can easily understand why the proposal was made verbally.
But, the most astonishing point is that this legislation, as I said a moment ago, not only includes the St. Laurent formula, which the Quebec provincial government rejected absolutely at all times, but even goes a step further in that it compels Quebec to return to Ottawa part of the money to be collected under provincial legislation for provincial purposes, and if it does not compel the province to return the money to Ottawa the federal government will see to it that the compensation is made.

I should say, to use an expression in favour with some Quebec members, that, from the constitutional standpoint, this is one of the most questionable pieces of legislation we have had since confederation.
As soon as the member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion) had made his speech, I very politely asked him a question to which he replied also very politely. I would like to remind him of it at this stage. I said, as reported on page 18 of the appendix to Hansard of April 26, 1960:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask a question of the hon. member for Bellechasse? If the hon. member for Bellechasse deems it completely constitutional to levy a provincial corporation tax for educational purposes, how can he explain that the federal government should, under the same bill, have the authority to compel the province of Quebec to return a portion of the same tax. Is that provision in the bill not the very contradiction of Mr. Cahan's statement?
The member for Bellechasse replied:
I am willing to assume that the hon. member has paid close attention to what I said. However, he leaves me with the impression that either I did not make myself clear or he misunderstood me. I rather believe that I was not quite clear.
At the beginning of my remarks, I very definitely stated that in my opinion the federal government is not allowed under the constitution to subsidize universities. I said that we were faced with an accomplished fact and that we try to evolve a temporary solution through a compromise. That is my view on the bill now before us.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Conservative members from Quebec who will speak after me-and the member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) will certainly be one of them-to tell us if the former premier of Quebec has ever accepted any compromise as far as the provincial autonomy of his province is concerned.
The Hon. Mr. Duplessis is known to have rejected federal university grants, except for one year, as I said a few moments ago. On the other hand, his minister of youth and welfare, the Hon. Paul Sauve, used to accept with open hands subsidies for technical and professional education, and annual grants for the maintenance and administration of his schools. Now, when federal grants were related to the building or installation of schools, they represented up to 50 per cent of the cost.
And when was any minister from Quebec heard telling the people of my province that the building costs of our technical and professional schools had been paid fifty-fifty by the federal government and the government

of Quebec? We were always led to believe, as we are being now, that those were princely gifts from the provincial government.
To my mind, Mr. Speaker, saying, when a school or a hospital or any public building is erected in some riding that it is a gift either of the federal or the provincial government, is misleading the people. Indeed, it is not a gift. It is merely a question of providing for the needs of the people where the building will be erected. And that is what I have always admired in our former prime minister; he never said that he was distributing gifts, but; "We are returning to the taxpayers part of the taxes they paid to the federal government".

We have heard before of grants to universities, Mr. Speaker, and by others than the federal government. Grants to universities have been awarded by the Quebec government to other institutions of higher learning in other provinces. I do not deny the right of the province of Quebec to help our fellow citizens in the other provinces. But what strikes me, again according to the principle of autonomy of our people in Quebec, is that the same Quebec government has awarded grants to institutions in other provinces. If the government of the province of Quebec had been logical and consistent with its theory on autonomy, it would have awarded those grants to a Quebec patriotic organization which would have handed them out to the interested people in the other provinces. No one would have been able to accuse the province of Quebec of interfering in the educational system of the other provinces, if it had followed that procedure.
Coming back to the agreements now being considered, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about the correspondence exchanged between the Prime Minister of Canada and the last two premiers-I repeat, the last two premiers-of the province of Quebec. On December 14, 1959, the Hon. Mr. Sauve, in an answer to the Prime Minister of Canada, asked this:
Dominion-Provincial Relations
You are suggesting that the adjustment be made out of the equalization payment. At least I suppose so, because it would be the only way to do it.
You would oblige me by saying if that is what you have in mind.
Here is what the Prime Minister of Canada answered to the Hon. Mr. Sauve on December 22, 1959:
The difference between the product of the additional 1 per cent tax exemption and the $1.50 per capita for the population of your province will be adjusted in such a way that the fiscal position of the federal government remains unchanged. In other words, should the 1 per cent tax exemption yield more than $1.50 per capita, as will be the case, the federal government will deduct the amount in excess of equalization payments now being paid to the province of Quebec by the federal treasury in accordance with the Federal-Provincial TaxSharing Arrangements Act.
For instance, if the new formula were applied on the basis of 1959 figures, the federal treasury would lose, and the provincial treasury gain, about $9,250,000 as a result of the change in the corporation tax. On the other hand, university grants based on $1.50 per capita, applied to the province of Quebec, would amount to $7,500,000. The difference of $1,750,000 would be deducted from the equalization payment payable to the province of Quebec which in- 1959 will amount to about $67,000,000.
There is another point on which I would like some clarification from the Conservative speakers who will rise after me. The Quebec legislature passed an act to raise from 9 to 10 per cent the corporation income tax before the federal government had introduced its own legislation. The provincial authorities knew at the time what were the three conditions laid down by the federal government concerning the use of provincial income tax.
I am at a loss to understand on the basis of what sincerity the Quebec government failed to mention in its legislation the conditions imposed by the federal government in order to dispose of a grant established by a provincial legislation for a provincial purpose.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, the Quebec provincial legislature as well as the federal authorities, entered into a tacit agreement before the Canadian parliament had expressed its views on the subject.
If this legislation had been introduced under a Liberal administration, with the restrictive clauses it contains, I am sure that Mr. Duplessis and all his supporters would have had a real picnic at the expense of the Liberal administration of the time.
In his speech on the federal grants to universities-and I want to say a few words about the remarks of the hon. member for

Dominion-Provincial Relations Bellechasse (Mr. Dorion)-the hon. member also expressed the views of a man who had been a student of constitutional law and who, according to him, was one of the most enlightened minds of his days; I mean Mr. Cahan, secretary of state in the Bennett administration. As did the hon. member for Bellechasse, I quote the following:
The provincial legislature will come to exercise, year by year, the Junctions of a municipal council which is dependent, in matters of finance, upon the benefactions which it receives from the federal treasury. The dominion government will hold the purse, and financial control will gradually extend to the exercise of legislative and administrative control.
Well, I believe the formula being proposed to us ties in fully with the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Bellechasse, and for the following reason: the province of Quebec will have to reimburse, or the federal government will deduct from the equalization payments, the excess amounts of taxes levied on corporations for provincial purposes.
I would not like to express an opinion neither officially nor oif the record on the constitutionality of the federal grants to universities because there are great jurists who hold different views on the matter. But I should like, however, to make a comparison. The special grants of $25 million which the federal government pays to the maritimes are not paid from a special tax levied throughout the country. Those special grants of $25 million are taken out of the federal treasury, like the university grants, as they were under Mr. St. Laurent's formula.
And there is another question I might ask myself about Quebec autonomists. There is, in the Department of Finance, in connection with federal-provincial relations, a municipal grant division. Municipalities, Mr. Speaker, in the eyes of the federal government, do not exist. The federal government does not recognize legally what a municipality is, because municipalities exist only by virtue of a delegation of powers from the provincial governments; and yet, grants are directly made to municipalities; cheques are made to the order of the municipalities. Those cheques are not sent to municipal officials, through the provincial government, they are sent directly to the municipalities of our province, and of all the other provinces of Canada.
How can you explain that the Conservative members from Quebec, who are so deeply

concerned with autonomy, have never raised the matter here in the House of Commons?

Mr. Speaker, there is something significant in this bill that struck us in the C.C.F. Here for the first time, at least in recent history, we have been able to come to an agreement on a very thorny problem in this country. For the first time, apparently, the federal government and the government of the province of Quebec have been able to reach an agreement on one of the most important subjects affecting the citizens of Canada regardless of the province in which they live. I refer to the problem of education.
I recall many times in the past how the Liberals used to pillory a former premier of the province of Quebec, Premier Duplessis. He was the fly in the ointment, the reason why that province would never take advantage of the many proposals put forward by the federal government. It was obvious to many in this country why he would not co-operate. It was more profitable politically to cry wolf in the province of Quebec when it came to any agreement with the federal government. It was also obvious for many years that the Quebec government was far more interested in votes than in agreements with respect to this problem.
We now see another strange phenomenon coming about. We see that we have a new Duplessis growing up in the province of Quebec. I have here a copy of an article taken from the Globe and Mail of April 14, which reads in parts as follows:
Quebec Liberal leader Jean Lesage said today that he will denounce the current federal-provincial agreement on the financing of university grants if his party takes power at the next general elections.
I do not know if he intends to denounce it only if his party takes power or if he
Dominion-Provincial Relations intends to denounce it in any event. As I understand the legislation, it does not ram anything down anybody's throat. It is merely permissive legislation allowing the minister to enter into an agreement with any province that desires to do so. Why denounce the agreement only if the party comes into power? The article continues:
Mr. Lesage said that the right given in the bill to the federal Minister of Finance to approve any arrangement between the provincial government and the universities constituted a most dangerous precedent in the field of provincial autonomy.
Shades of Duplessis. I have studied this proposal and fail to see how anybody could construe as a dangerous precedent in the field of provincial autonomy the fact that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has the authority to approve an arrangement between the provincial governments and the universities. Surely this is under provincial jurisdiction. If they reach an agreement who is treading on whose toes if the federal government is authorized to approve it? Another portion of the article reads:
Mr. Lesage said that this policy of federal-provincial fiscal relations would constitute a major theme of the Liberal campaign during the next two months.
The Union Nationale will be attacked for not sticking to the autonomist position taken by Duplessis and Sauve in their relations with Ottawa.
Why did we hear the Liberals for so many years attack the position taken by Mr. Duplessis if they are now going to attack his successors for not following the position he took? What kind of monstrous farce is this?
For many years there has been a great game in this country played by politicians. The game consisted of making one political speech in Quebec and a different one in any other province. With the advent of television and the establishment of the C.B.C. in Canada the game is not as easily played as before because speeches of importance are telecast from coast to coast and one cannot indulge in double-talk and give both sides of the picture. This is particularly true with respect to the subject of education.
I submit that for 92 years we have coasted and quibbled with regard to education and I think it is time we stopped. This first agreement on the question is a good starting point and that is why the C.C.F. intends to support the bill on second reading.
I invite hon. members to consider how many qualified students have been denied opportunities for education in years gone by. Why? Because education has been a

Dominion-Provincial Relations political football kicked back and forth between the federal and provincial governments each saying it was the responsibility of the other. And because all the provinces could not agree, it was a good way of washing one's hands of the subject. I invite the house to consider the human resources that have been wasted as a result of our washing our hands of this problem.
Of course, we have been very lucky. While we have never tried to meet the problem or provide adequate opportunities for education to our students as they grew up, fortunately our educational system was no worse than the systems in other countries and so we had no real problems to face up to. But times are changing very rapidly. One has only to consider automation to realize that the standards of education which were adequate 10 or 15 years ago are no longer adequate today.
This afternoon we had an exchange between the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough) and the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), I believe, with regard to unfilled job applications. I think there is something in what the minister said about many positions being unfilled at this time. Why is this so? Because our workers have not got the educational qualifications to fill them.
What are we doing about it? We are playing petty politics instead of getting on with the job. How many of our students are demanding educational opportunities today while we sit here and kick this matter back and forth? I see that the Quebec election battle is going to be fought on the basis of the same old worn out excuse on which elections in Quebec have been fought for the last number of years. Do we realize, Mr. Speaker, that while we indulge ourselves in these political antics immigrants coming into this country are better qualified to fill jobs than our own people born and raised here? Do we realize that this situation is going to worsen unless we stop bickering and playing petty politics and get on with the job of increasing educational facilities and educational opportunities for our children?
Last but far from least, Mr. Speaker, are we going to sit back and ignore the warnings from behind the iron curtain that were so well put before the house by two members on the government side last year? Can we afford to do this? Are we still going to quibble and play party politics?
The British North America Act sets out very clearly provincial and federal rights

with regard to education but unfortunately it does not set out the responsibilities as clearly as it should. It is the responsibility of each province to provide educational facilities and because some provinces are richer than others it is the responsibility of the federal government to see that each province is able to carry out its educational responsibilities. As I said before, in the past there has been no over-all agreement. We have been content to pass the buck back and forth. The attitude has been, anything for an excuse, let us shut our eyes and avoid the inevitable for a few years longer and maybe we can win another election by doing so.
I say that we have a far greater responsibility with regard to this problem. I say that this welcome step is the first step we have seen for a good many years in this field. I say it is time that provincial and federal elected representatives started to place national and human interests ahead of immediate political ambitions. I say it is time that we got on with this welcome first step and go on from here to even greater steps in the future. (Translation):

Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be brief, because what is well understood can be expressed in few words.
The problem of federal subsidies to universities is one of vital importance in my province, and has been for close to 20 years. It involves, as we all know, an intrusion of the central power into the provincial field. Under section 93 of the B.N.A. Act, only the provincial legislatures have jurisdiction in educational matters. It can be truly said that until the publication of the Massey report on June 1, 1951, the federal government had never committed a constitutional sin in that respect.
The Massey commission, which on the whole did quite a good job, suggested in its report that the federal government should make a financial contribution to the work of universities every year. The commissioners put it that clearly. That was reason enough for the Liberal government of the time to accept this unwarranted suggestion, and shortly after, it started making annual inroads into the field of education.
From that point of view, it can be said that the government which preceded the present government was a second offender and persisted in its constitutional sin. There were ministers in Quebec who defended such a

policy. Among them, I would mention the former minister of northern affairs and national resources, Mr. Jean Lesage, who in the meantime has changed his tune and is trying to go into reverse. However, a choice replacement was found in the person of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) who has been making sudden and occasional T.V. appearances in Quebec. Let me say, however, that I think his national patriotic speeches have a hollow sound: he is a bit like a banjo player in a symphony orchestra.
To set the problem in its proper perspective, it must be remembered that very few countries enjoy the advantages of two cultures. In that respect, Canada is a privileged country.
In fact, because of historic events which have made Canada what it is today, we enjoy French culture with all its beauty, its richness, its dignity and its greatness. At the same time, we enjoy Anglo-Saxon culture in all its beauty, its richness, its dignity and its greatness. Each in their own sphere, French speaking and English speaking Canadians can benefit by developing their cultures whose full flowering can only enrich our national heritage.
To get this full flowering, Quebec universities, which are the guardians of French culture in America, need greater financial assistance. And who could legally give it to them? We find the answer in section 93 of the British North America Act: Only the provincial legislatures, since they have exclusive jurisdiction in the field of education.
I do not think there are right minded people, with the exception, perhaps of the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge), who would say that universities are not included in this field. If this is a responsibility of provincial legislatures, they need adequate financial means to discharge it. So, what did the Quebec government do in order to be able to give financial assistance to our universities? During its last session, the Quebec legislature raised the corporation income tax by 1 per cent. The sums produced by this increase will enable Quebec universities to receive the financial assistance they are entitled to. The present federal government, always anxious, and may I repeat that, always anxious to respect the autonomy of the provinces, refuses to remain any longer, against the will of the province, in the field of education, and will grant a similar deduction from its own tax. In other words, the federal
Dominion-Provincial Relations government is gradually withdrawing from a field which is not its own, and which was invaded in 1951 by the Liberal government.
On behalf of the citizens of Quebec, I commend the present federal government for showing great understanding and an admittedly fair mind.
I know you will realize, Mr. Speaker, that the member for an historic county like Montmagny-L'Islet, wants to pay a disinterested tribute to the man who is now the premier of the province of Quebec and who, today, picks the ripe fruit of the long and difficult struggles led by his illustrious predecessors. Yet, I am sure that, if the Quebec government had formerly been able to count on the comprehension and co-operation of the Liberal government, it could have settled the problem quite as beneficially. Because of its arrogance and stubbornness, the Liberal government found itself, so to speak, in an extremely difficult position. How many great men fought all their lives, and even died, before reaping the fruit of their efforts.
Mr. Speaker, about a week ago, the hon. member for Laurier honoured us with a visit. He spoke on television, in a program entitled: "The Nation's Business". Besides, one finds that he is about the only Liberal member to appear on the French network. I do not blame him for wanting to make himself known among our people but his frequent appearances might suggest that he is somewhat hard to sell.
The last time he appeared on television the hon. member for Laurier told us that Bill No. C-56 was the worst encroachment on provincial autonomy. He said that by this Bill No. C-56 the federal government was saying to the legislature: "You will increase the corporation tax by 1 per cent. The hon. member knows very well that this is not true. If he does not know, let him examine the text of the bill and study it carefully. If he knows that he is not speaking the truth, why does he come to the province of Quebec and say things which are, to say the least, contrary to the truth? The fact is that the Quebec legislature voted its bill increasing the corporation tax without being the least concerned with what the federal government would do. The Hon. Antonio Barrette formally said so in Montreal, on April 19 last. To avoid double taxation and, as I said, out of regard for the autonomy of the provinces, the federal government will grant a 1 per cent deduction on its own tax. I wonder who could criticize it for that?

Dominion-Provincial Relations
I listened earlier with great interest to my very good and long time friend, the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard). He said, at one point, that the proof that grants to universities are constitutional and legal is that they were accepted in 1951 by the province of Quebec.
Let me remind him of a minor principle of law that he must have learned when he was a law student in Quebec. He says that in the matter of evidence one must of necessity abide by the principle of preponderance. Correct, the province of Quebec tentatively accepted university grants the first year. However, when the province refused them the following year, and has refused them ever since, the preponderance of evidence is to the effect that it had come to the conclusion that the experiment made in 1951 had not proved to be a useful compromise under those conditions.
I also heard the hon. member exclaiming while speaking about his late protector Mr. Duplessis, that he had never accepted any compromise. Let me tell him that there is one very simple reason why the then premier of Quebec never accepted any compromise; it is because he knew how dangerous it is to compromise oneself with a Liberal government.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, may I tell you that we breathe more freely in our province since the government of Quebec can rely on the comprehension and the co-operation of the federal Conservative government.
The era of liberal arrogance and of the "take it or leave it" attitude of Mr. St. Laurent is now a thing of the past, and we already see on the horizon a future full of splendid promises which will represent a precious contribution to the full achievement of that national unity which we desire and which will enrich our national life and make it worthy of the most noble traditions-as the Prime Minister of Canada stated when General de Gaulle visited our country-of both our mother countries, France and Great Britain.

Mr. Speaker, there are two proposals in the bill now before this house. The first one has to do with an increase from 10 to 13 per cent in the provincial share of personal income tax. It will be recalled that the increase came into effect in January 1958 and was announced by wire to the provinces. The object of this bill is to keep the increase in force up to March 31, 1962 or for two more years.

The second proposal concerns arrangements on grants to universities, concerning which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) stated that the amendment is to provide for the payment of grants to universities equivalent to $1.50 per capita in each province.
Let me state forthwith, as did the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) on April 26 last, that I am in favour of the first proposal. However, I think it proper to point out that, since the Conservatives came into power three years ago, nothing was changed in the Federal-Provincial Tax-sharing Arrangements Act, except the 3 per cent increase in private income tax which enables us to say that under the Conservative administration we have autonomy at 3 per cent.
Since June 1957, three federal-provincial conferences have been held, but each of them almost uselessly because every time the premiers and the ministers of finance of the ten provinces went back empty-handed. I am not the only one to make this statement. An editorial in Le Soleil, for October 17, 1959, was entitled:
Useless Conference.
The article reads as follows:
Gathered in Ottawa to discuss with the federal Minister of Finance problems concerning the taxsharing arrangements, the ministers of finance of the ten provinces of this country and the few premiers who came along with them, went back empty-handed forty eight hours later.
If they had any hopes before entering the conference room, they did not keep them long. Mr. Fleming hastened to tell them they would not be getting anything more because the country's financial situation made it impossible.
The article goes on to say this, and rightly so:
Was it really necessary to disturb all those people? Would it not have been simpler to cancel the conference and to inform each provincial minister of finance by mail to expect nothing more from the federal treasury? In this way, there would have been no loss of time, no wasteful expenditures, no useless travelling.
The representatives of the provinces did not hide their disappointment and their displeasure.
We are being told that another federal-provincial conference has been set for next July, on the 25, 26 and 27. However, judging from past conferences and the statement made by the Minister of Finance on April 26, 1960, as recorded in Hansard page 3278 of that day:
The matters to be submitted to the conference will concern financial relations between the dominion and the provinces in the period following March 31, 1962.

We must therefore conclude that no change will be made in the tax-sharing arrangements between the dominion and the provinces before March 31, 1962.
And yet, Mr. Speaker, that is not what the Conservative party gave us to understand during the electoral campaign of 1957 and 1958. The present Prime Minister said at St. Patrice de Beaurivage, in the province of Quebec, on May 30, 1957, according to a report in the June 1, 1957 issue of the daily newspaper Montreal-Matin, and I quote:
The head of the Conservative party tackled another serious problem: that of fiscal federal-provincial relations. "Everybody admits", he said, "that relations between Ottawa and the provinces are bad, and that they are not satisfactory either to provincial or to municipal administrations. The federal government is rich, but the provinces and the municipalities are poor, and they cannot continue to assume their responsibilities.
"To resume the attitude of our party", he stated. "I repeat what I have said at the start of the election campaign: We guarantee provinces and municipalities a greater share of the money raised by taxes.
We shall thus give provincial governments the means of shouldering their important constitutional responsibilities and of furthering the development of our natural resources."
I might, Mr. Speaker, quote many other statements along this line, made by the Prime Minister and his candidates about fiscal arrangements during the 1957 and 1958 elections; but I think that the one I just mentioned will be enough to show that the Conservatives always acted grandly in their promises but rather poorly when it came to carrying them out.
Is it not pitiful to see a government, which, with the help of its friends in Quebec, organized two campaigns against the fiscal formula of the St. Laurent government, doing absolutely nothing today but modify some figures very slightly, which the Liberals might have done too, as one of the main merits of that formula was the possibility of periodical adjustment of standards according to the needs of the hour.
The greatest sin of the Conservatives is not their present reluctance to solve the fiscal problem; it is the boldness with which, for the sole purpose of grabbing power, they made to the people, in two elections, extravagant promises they are now unable to fulfil.
Nothing is easier to understand than the reason why the Conservative government does not solve the fiscal problem: it is because the Liberals have solved it as much
Dominion-Provincial Relations as they could, at the time, and the Conservatives are absolutely unable to find a more efficient and fairer formula than that adopted by the Liberals.
Through work and intelligence, the St. Laurent government had developed a fiscal formula which was severely criticized by his opponents, but will remain in force as long as a better one has not been found, and none is yet in sight.
On this subject, I should like to quote from an article by Gerard Morin, which appeared in Le Droit of Ottawa for July 8, 1959 under the heading: "No new contribution from Duplessis at the conference." This refers to the conference of the committee of Canadian finance ministers and treasurers, held in Ottawa in early July of the same year. I quote:
It seems that the federal Conservative government, which in principle is friendly to the government of the same party in Quebec, is not an inch closer to an agreement with Mr. Duplessis than the former government. In fact, the Conservatives have made no change in the Liberal doctrine of tax agreements, which the present Quebec government has always described as a centralizing doctrine.
Mr. Duplessis, in his Monday night press conference boasted of having repeated the same thing he had said for about 15 years in Ottawa, that-
And this is for the information of the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard).
-that Ottawa was robbing Quebec.
And to a reporter who asked Mr. Duplessis if he had made constructive suggestions to the conference. he answered with his usual wit: "When someone robs us, nothing is more constructive than to claim back the amount that was robbed."
Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, those words were said not only at the time of the Liberals, but after the provincial treasurers' conference held early last July. Our Conservative friends, more particularly in Quebec, are therefore-* after this last remark of their political idol in July 1959-unable to claim that they have brought about any change in the formula set up by the Liberal party, which they denounced so loudly and which they were to change so quickly. They therefore have to admit their complete failure on that point. It was indeed stated by Lorenzo Pare, parliamentary correspondent of L'Action Catho-lique, in a report published in that paper on November 26, 1957, the day after the first federal-provincial conference, and I quote:
If some people still pretended to believe that the coming of the Diefenbaker government would bring about a reversal of fiscal and financial policy in Ottawa, the end of the system of grants to the provinces and a new concept of constitutional relations; the illusion they nurtured would have disappeared yesterday.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
Not only does the centralization of the three major taxes remain the basis of federal policies, but those policies are more immediately directed to the fields where provincial jurisdiction was until now undivided.
Mr. Speaker, I do not say that the formula advanced by the Liberal government was perfect and that no changes should be made to it. It should certainly be studied again with a view to improving it and to making it more suitable to the needs and conditions which have changed tremendously since confederation days. But such a complex problem in a country like ours, cannot, to my mind, be solved as long as we do not decide to approach it with an open and constructive mind and acting with reason and frankness. It seems to me, that on such a vital question, we should all have a common ideal, to work for the greatness and advancement of our municipalities, provinces and our country as a whole.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about the second proposal included in this bill, that is, the one concerning university grants.
It has been pointed out during this debate, and even in previous debates, that, for several years, higher learning in Canada has been faced with a very serious financial situation, which was approaching a state of crisis, in the sense that it could no longer fulfil its role in this field. I think I can say we are unanimous on this point.
Faced with such a situation, the government of Mr. St. Laurent rightly decided to help solve that crisis. Therefore, during the 1951 session, it arranged for the adoption of yearly grants to universities, on the basis of 50 cents per capita. Those federal grants to universities were accepted by all parties then sitting in the house, and afterwards by all provinces. Furthermore, those grants, as we know, are made directly to universities recognized as such by provincial governments.
After allowing the universities of the province of Quebec to accept that assistance for the first year only, the provincial authorities in my province withdrew that permission in 1952, under the pretext that they were afraid it was a first encroachment upon the exclusive jurisdiction of provincial legislatures in the field of education.
All members who were sitting in this house in June 1951, when that assistance was announced and adopted on the thirtieth of the same month, will recall that the leaders of the two major parties, while recognizing the

jurisdiction of the provinces in the field of education, admitted that the formula was constitutional. Mr. St. Laurent, in announcing the measure, said this, as recorded on page 4278 of Hansard tor June 19, 1951, and I quote:
I might add that in making these recommendations to parliament it is intended to avoid any possible suggestion that we are interfering in any way with the policies respecting education in the respective provinces.
On the thirtieth of the same month, in the discussion on item 690, which dealt with grants to universities, here is what he said, as recorded on page 5021 of Hansard:
What is intended is that all the institutions, authorized by provincial legislatures to grant degrees, would be recognized as of university level
Now here is what the then Conservative leader, Hon. Mr. Drew, had to say, as recorded on page 4278 of Hansard for June 19, 1951:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon. members generally will welcome any measure of assistance given in this way to the universities of Canada... on behalf of the party X have the privilege to lead I proposed some time ago that these grants should be made as soon as possible-
Mr. Speaker, I think those words clearly show that there was perfect unanimity on the federal government's right to award grants to universities. As you know, such grants were unconditional and in no way contrary to section 93 of the constitution, which provides that: "In each province, the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to education". In voting that estimate, parliament in no way claimed the right to legislate in the field of education, or to determine the curricula or define the school attendance requirements to which their citizens would be subjected.
Nor did it impose a direct tax in the province in order to obtain revenues for school purposes. All the federal government was doing was to offer grants to universities from the consolidated revenue fund of Canada.
It seems to me that, under the circumstances, I can join with others, even if I am not known as an authority in this field, in saying-
May I ask a question to the hon. member?

I have no objection. I will first finish my speech and, once I am through, I will be glad to answer your question.
Therefore, I can say with many others, without being an expert in constitutional matters, that those federal grants had no effect whatsoever on the autonomy of the

universities or the provinces. Besides, it is because of that same right that the federal government makes equalization payments to provincial governments, helps in financing hospital construction, helps in technical and professional education, these latest grants having been accepted by the province of Quebec from 1945 to 1958.
Why then would the grants paid to the universities by the Liberals be bad, while the others I just mentioned are accepted? If the Quebec government believes that those grants which have been paid for nine years, now, are unconstitutional, why did it not challenge their legality before the courts?
This question has to be answered by the Conservative members.
In his speech of last April 26, the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) said this, as reported at page 1 of the appendix to Hansard of that day:
Besides, why should we have entrusted to provincial governments the exclusive power of looking after education, if the educational system had been the same in all the provinces which were to become members of the confederation?
Well, Mr. Speaker, I think it is agreed that the fathers of confederation placed education under the exclusive control of the provinces, probably with a view to safeguarding both English and French cultures. But to this moment, nobody has shown yet that the federal grants to universities, as conceived by the St. Laurent government, could be a threat either to the French culture or to the English culture, or even to the various religions in Canada.
Let us talk now about the new system proposed by this government. I feel that it would be useless to repeat the sound arguments presented by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) in the remarkable speech he made on that question, last April 26. He made it clear, I think, with references to various legislations and judgments of the Supreme Court of Canada, that certain parts of this bill can constitute the worst interference ever attempted by a federal government into the affairs of a province.
Besides, he is not the only one to entertain such views. I have here an editorial written by Mr. Gerard Filion in the Montreal newspaper Le Devoir of January 16, 1960, which reads as follows:
The Diefenbaker proposal, it should be remembered, is worse in its principle than the Liberal government's formula. That one, at least, set no conditions to universities or to provinces. Money was paid out and that was all. Whereas Mr. Diefenbaker is willing to have the provinces collect a certain amount of money, provided that it be used a certain way and not beyond certain limits.

I also have another item from Quebec's Le Soleil, dated December 18, 1959, which has the following heading:
The Diefenbaker proposal is deemed unacceptable by the Montreal chamber of commerce.
May I now quote a few paragraphs from an item headed:
Direct Interference
Furthermore, it brings about direct interference by the federal government in provincial matters by telling the provinces how they are to use their own tax money. It is, therefore, no uncertain breach of a constitutional principle to which Quebec holds fast.
One could even say that by accepting the method suggested we should be worse off than before. Federal grants to universities at the present time, though questionable from the constitutional standpoint, involve no interference in provincial jurisdiction.
It might well be pointed out at this time that the Conservative party arrived at this solution only after two years and a half in power, and yet its own supporters in this house called it a poor arrangement and an imperfect formula. I rather think that if those involved and all the students in the province had not pressed the government into action and, moreover, if this had not been a provincial election year, the Conservative party would have kept on distributing university grants according to the St. Laurent formula.
I also wonder how the Conservative members from the province of Quebec who consider Mr. St. Laurent's formula as infringing upon provincial autonomy can vote for the bill in which that same formula is included.
In an article written in the newspaper La Presse by its Ottawa correspondent Mr. Amedee Gaudreault on January 25, 1960, I read this:
The bill including the Diefenbaker formula concerning federal grants to universities, after the letter sent by the Hon. Antonio Barrette to the Prime Minister of Canada, is expected to force the 50 federal conservative members from Quebec to do some soul-searching in comparison to which the hesitations and abstentions of last year on the fiscal agreements and the trans-Canada highway will seem trifling.
Mr. Speaker, I find it strange, like many people from the province of Quebec, that Mr. Duplessis' followers in this house can talk about compromise when autonomy is concerned, because Mr. Duplessis always said that he would never permit autonomy to be crucified even on a golden cross.
If for many years the Union Nationale leaders and their friends from the province of Quebec had cast aside petty politics and emotionalism and had shown more common

I need not point out, Mr. Speaker, in closing my remarks that the Liberals' attitude towards federal grants to universities has not changed.
They are in favor of those grants unconditionally. Whether they are distributed by the Canadian Universities Foundation or, as the member for Laurier suggested, by a provincial council of universities, is of no importance, but I raise serious doubts as to the constitutionality of the formula introduced in this bill.
I hope that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) will clear up the serious doubts raised about the constitutionality of some clauses of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) who today not only shoulders his own responsibilities but also those of Prime Minister. The hon. member realizes that we have a constitution. In contrast with the Liberals, he recognizes that provinces have rights of their own. Moreover, he does much to unite the main elements which constitute our nation and to improve the conditions existing between our central government and provincial governments.
Mr. Speaker, this is not the least surprising, for the Conservative party, under the present leadership of the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, has done a lot since confederation, and is still doing a lot, in order to ensure a better understanding of provincial rights and to maintain good will between the central government and all provincial governments.

It would seem to me that in a day and age when government is becoming larger and larger at all levels, federal, provincial and municipal, and when the government itself at each of these levels is, perhaps, intervening in our daily lives to a greater and greater extent, we in this House of Commons should devote great attention to what are generally described as dominion-provincial relations.
I have not as yet reached the exalted position, which it seems to me some of the hon. members alongside me have reached, of quoting past speeches that I have made in this house, but I would simply like to say that I pointed out during the budget debate that one of the real differences which divide the two main parties in this chamber relates to dominion-provincial relations.
I pointed out in my speech on that occasion that our party places a great deal of emphasis on what is termed, for lack of a better expression, local self-agency. This idea has a universal application to Conservative principles. I fully realize that we cannot import into Canada political doctrines from nations abroad, but we do not all have to be students of history to look at the problems of the Liberals in the United Kingdom and the trouble the opposition had there not so many

years ago. I do not intend to embark on a Port Arthur type lecture in this House of Commons. Nevertheless, we realize the trouble the United Kingdom got into at the end of the last century when the Liberals over there tried to centralize affairs in London. Again, I am not suggesting you can import political doctrines, but it would certainly seem to me in the light of modern past experience in this country that the Liberal party, even though hon. members of that party do not like to admit it, have inherited a great deal of the whig's centralizing traditions of the past.
Only the other day the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) was asked down in Washington why the Liberal party was turned out of power. He gave as his answer that the Canadian people became bored with perfection. I am certain that many hon. members on this side of the house at least are going to have a great deal to say about the remark made by the Leader of the Opposition perhaps in a moment of carelessness, outside the borders of this country. Let me reiterate right now: I see nothing that smacks of perfection regarding the Liberal party's attitude and performance in relation to dominion-provincial relations as such.
I well remember during the last session of parliament that the Leader of the Opposition showed notable chagrin and was extremely annoyed when an hon. member on this side of the house brought up the fact that in order to unite this country in a true fashion we had to recognize the fact that various provinces had different attitudes. In other words, the word "diversity" was used. The Leader of the Opposition was highly annoyed that the subject had even come up in the House of Commons. His annoyance was heightened by the fact that we suggested that everybody should recognize the diversity of the provincial elements making up this country from coast to coast. Let him be annoyed and chagrined but the facts are these, that the divide and rule policies and programs carried out by the Liberal party in this house and throughout the country during the past years and that party's centralist tendencies leave absolutely no room for the recognition of provincial diversity. As a matter of fact the centralist tendencies of hon. gentlemen opposite-and this is an important principle to get over and underline during this present debate-tend to dragoon Canadians in the name of uniformity.
I would be the first to admit that during the war years and post-war years we had emergencies and semi-emergencies with their obvious accompanying centralizing effects. We do not have to read many periodicals and indeed we have only to look abroad to see 79951-0-225J
Dominion-Provincial Relations that certain political leaders and statesmen are trying now to create emergency or semiemergency conditions in order to centralize powers.
The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) often wonders why I changed my political allegiance. I can only say to the hon. member that I was never one who subscribed very much to the Howe theory of eternal emergency with its centralizing effects, another concept which I think hon. members alongside do not like to have brought up again and again, but I believe the time has come when they have to admit the basic policies that they adopt in relation to the problem of dominion-provincial relations. We know of one hon. member of the other place who mentioned the fact that his party adopted a policy of pragmatism and expediency and this applies to their attitude in this field.
I do not think the Canadian people will ever forget the debt they owe to the opposition of that time for their performance during the emergency powers debate not so many, years ago when complete powers forever were asked for in this Canadian House of Commons-
Does my hon. friend remember that on that very occasion the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) disgraced himself to his lasting disadvantage?

Well, I withdraw the question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. Nevertheless it is interesting for me to note that apart from the present formal debate we are having in this House of Commons, it is usually the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate

Dominion-Provincial Relations (Mr. Pickersgill) who sallies forth into the waters of dominion-provincial relations. I have noticed that not too many of the hon. members on the front benches of the official opposition-not even the hon. member for Essex East with his usual expertise-has ventured forth into these waters.
The hon. member for Essex East has been sick.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think he is still sick.

I believe it was during the resolution stage of this debate that the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) brought the following set of facts. to the attention of hon. members of this house. He said that when the Liberal party was in power and was advocating the acceptance by the provinces of university grants all hon. members supporting the party of which I am a member said they were no good and that this should not be done. Today the hon. member claims that the present government made up of hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party is advocating the acceptance by the provinces of university grants and now we say they are all right. To a large extent the statement made by the hon. member is correct because during the time of the Liberal reign they tried to superimpose their will on the provinces with a take it or leave it attitude. There was no acceptance method worked out through consultation with the provinces. Just as they forgot the people of the country, they forgot the necessity of consultation on questions of this real and grave importance. Today the difference is that an acceptable method has been worked out by consultation with the provinces-
By telegram.

-by a party that realizes the provinces have their constitutional rights. That is the difference, Mr. Speaker. For that reason I will admit that a lot of what was said by the hon. member for St. Jean-Iber-ville-Napierville was correct, but I want to tell the hon. member why today we are in essence supporting this bill as opposed to the attitude we took while in opposition.
It is because you have a strong whip.

We have a very excellent whip, Mr. Speaker, who is appreciated and enjoyed by all hon. members of this party of which I am a member. I suggest he perhaps does not use the same dragooning techniques that characterized some of the whips of the previous Liberal administration because I understand that in past days the backbench members of the Liberal party in this house were not too much encouraged by Mr. Howe to get up and express themselves to any extent.
How many dissenters are there in the hon. member's party now?
Pardon?

I asked the hon. gentleman, Mr. Speaker, if he would name the dissenters there are in his party right now, apart from the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Van Horne) who has been practically kicked out of the door.
We are a united team, Mr. Speaker, going ahead together in the best interests of our country. May I call it six o'clock?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I inquire what the business is for tomorrow and Friday? I understand it was announced yesterday and I presume there is no change but I wonder if the house leader would be good enough to indicate what we might be doing next week.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Next week's program, Mr. Speaker, I think could be more properly announced tomorrow night. For tomorrow, Thursday, this debate will continue. If it is terminated we will take the budget resolutions. On Friday we will take the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.
May I ask whether since last night any consideration has been given as to when the debate on the abolition of capital punishment will continue?
